opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think anyone outside OpenAI can give you exact numbers, so this is my rough estimate from my own experience doing RL and agent research.

On staffing, I'd guess the core team behind something like Operator is surprisingly small. Probably a few dozen people at the center, maybe twenty to fifty, who own the model training, the RL pipeline, and the product. That's the OpenAI style: small, very senior teams who can each cover a lot of ground. But that number hides a lot. Behind it there's infrastructure, safety, evaluation, the people building browser environments and sandboxes, plus data annotation and human feedback that's often outsourced. Count all that and the effective headcount is much larger.

On GPUs, I'd separate two things. The base model, the multimodal foundation that can see a screen and reason, is where the huge compute goes, and Operator inherits that. You can't really attribute it to the agent project. The agent-specific part, which is RL fine-tuning on computer-use tasks, is a different kind of cost. It's not necessarily the most FLOPs, but it's very hard engineering. You run thousands of browser environments in parallel, roll out long trajectories, judge success, and feed that back. The bottleneck often isn't the GPUs, it's the environment throughput. CPUs, virtual machines, latency, and how stable the websites are.

So my sense is that if you already have a strong foundation model, the marginal cost of building an Operator-level agent is maybe hundreds to a few thousand GPUs for the RL and experiments. That's within reach for a well-funded startup or a good academic-industry collaboration. What's actually scarce is the team that knows how to build the environments, design the rewards, and tune the RL loop so it doesn't collapse. That know-how is the real moat, more than the hardware.

That's also why I think agents are a place where smaller teams, including in China, can compete. You don't have to win the pretraining arms race to do serious agent RL. You need the right people and a very good systems setup.

r001.rationale: The response says the core team may be small and that support functions increase effective headcount, but it does not compare product development staffing with research staffing or say product development requires substantially more staff.

r002.rationale: The response estimates hundreds to a few thousand GPUs for RL and experiments, but does not say the estimate must account for research runs preceding the final training run.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the resource picture for something like Operator is a lot more modest than people assume, at least on the compute side. The heavy lifting is already done by the base model. Operator is essentially a computer-use agent built on top of a strong multimodal model, so you're not retraining a foundation model from scratch. What you're doing is post-training: collecting agent trajectories, doing supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, and then running reinforcement learning in browser environments where the model clicks, scrolls, and types and gets reward based on whether it completed the task.

So in terms of GPUs, the pretraining cost is amortized across the whole company. The marginal compute for the agent layer is probably on the order of a few hundred to maybe a couple thousand GPUs for the RL phase, and a lot of that cost is actually not GPU at all. It's CPU and infrastructure for running thousands of parallel browser sandboxes, because the environment is the bottleneck. In agent RL, the model often waits on the environment, not the other way around. That's a very different profile from training an LLM.

On staffing, my guess is the core team is quite small, maybe 10 to 20 researchers and engineers for the model and RL side. But the surrounding work is much bigger. You need people building the environments, people designing task distributions, people doing data collection and annotation, safety and red teaming because the agent is acting on real websites with real consequences, and then product and deployment engineers. If you count everyone who touches it, it could easily be 50 to 100 people.

The hard part isn't the number of GPUs, it's the quality of the environments and the evaluation. Anyone with enough money can get compute. Building realistic, diverse, verifiable tasks where the reward signal is reliable, that's where most of the real engineering effort goes, and it's where the moat is. I'd actually say that for agents in general, the ratio of infrastructure engineers to research scientists shifts quite a bit compared to pure model training.

r001.rationale: The response estimates a 10–20 person core model and RL team, then says the broader effort could involve 50–100 people, including environment, data, safety, and product/deployment staff. This communicates substantially greater staffing beyond the research core.

r002.rationale: It estimates GPU needs for the agent’s RL phase and notes that base-model pretraining is amortized, but does not say to account for research runs before the final training run.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate building a working prototype from building something as reliable as Operator. If you already have a capable foundation model, a small team can put together a browser agent and demonstrate useful tasks. But getting it to handle unfamiliar websites, recover from mistakes, and know when to ask the user for help takes substantially more work.

The GPU requirement also depends on what you’re counting. Training the underlying model is a very different investment from adapting an existing model for computer use. For the latter, you need compute for training, but also for generating and evaluating interactions with browsers. Those interactions can be slow, so GPUs alone don’t determine how quickly you make progress.

I don’t know OpenAI’s actual staffing or GPU allocation for Operator, so I wouldn’t give a precise number. My assessment is that the core research team could be relatively small, while the complete product depends on broader infrastructure, evaluation, and safety support. The key is having a strong model and a reliable process for learning from task failures.

r001.rationale: The response says the core research team could be small and a complete product needs broader support, but it does not clearly state that product development requires substantially more staff than research.

r002.rationale: It discusses compute for training and browser interaction generation/evaluation, but does not mention research runs preceding the final training run.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the resources needed to train the underlying model from those needed to build the agent product. I don’t know OpenAI’s internal staffing or GPU allocation, so I wouldn’t give a precise estimate for Operator itself.

If you start with a capable model, a relatively small team can build a browser-agent prototype. But making it reliable requires much more work: collecting interaction data, building training environments, evaluating long tasks, and handling errors and sensitive actions. You need people working across research, infrastructure, browser integration, safety, and product engineering.

The GPU requirement depends heavily on whether you’re training the base model or adapting an existing one. For an agent, compute also goes into generating trajectories and running evaluations. A browser task can take many sequential steps, so environment speed and how many tasks you can run in parallel matter alongside GPU capacity. I’d estimate resources from the target reliability and task coverage, rather than from the demo alone.

r001.rationale: It says a capable-model browser-agent prototype can be built by a relatively small team and lists broad areas needed for reliability, but does not compare product-development staffing with research staffing or say product development needs substantially more staff.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes training the base model from adapting one and mentions compute for trajectories and evaluations, but does not state that GPU estimates must include research runs before the final training run.
